A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRIVBENCH/PRIVTUNE research despite the changed title and organization. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original VLM evaluations, privacy-tuning experiments, ablations, human label-quality assessments, and analysis of 100,000 Places365 images.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds VISPR evaluations and benchmark-resampling results.

M1.justification: Privacy VLM is the renamed TinyLLaVA + PRIVTUNE model. Both versions describe the same label-conditioned GPT-4/ShareGPT dialogue generation and LoRA fine-tuning procedure; no new architecture, objective, or algorithmic component is established.

E1.justification: v3 adds VISPR as a principal evaluation benchmark and includes it in the human label audit. Its broader attribute-based privacy taxonomy, including appearance, personal-life, and contextual information, substantially extends the external validation. Earlier datasets, multilingual tests, and Places365 coverage remain.

E2.justification: The same ten VLM comparators remain in corresponding benchmark comparisons, including Fuyu, CoAgent, and zero-shot TinyLLaVA. VISPR uses this existing comparator set; additional dataset citations do not introduce evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: v3 replaces F1 with MCC as the primary metric and adds balanced accuracy and specificity. It introduces evaluation on 100 random half-benchmark subsets. Reported human-study instructions change from withholding the study purpose to explaining it, and Table 10 tightens nudity and private-chat inclusion rules. These documented revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds a benchmark-size stability analysis and VISPR quality analyses using human judgments, DETR detections, and attribute examples. It removes the numerical CLIP diversity comparison and the brief report of unsuccessful in-context/chain-of-thought experiments. The principal class-exclusion, training-data-size, multilingual, and Places365 analyses already existed.

E5.justification: v3 Table 6 newly reports MCC means and standard deviations across 100 random 50% PRIVBENCH subsets for four models. This is a bounded addition of performance-variability reporting, not evidence of 100 independent training runs. Existing dialogue statistics and inter-rater agreement reporting remain.

E6.justification: v3 adds VISPR results, extensive MCC results, and resampling statistics; VISPR MCC is 0.35 for Privacy VLM versus 0.27 for CoAgent. Most retained aggregate F1 scores persist, but Privacy VLM's PrivAlert F1/precision/recall change from 0.62/0.51/0.80 in v2 Table 9 to 0.63/0.54/0.76 in v3 Table 14. These are revised reported outcomes; metric changes and incomplete setting correspondence preclude treating them as demonstrated version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The custom CLIP-based diversity-score definition in v2 Section 4 is removed. The binary privacy formulation, dialogue-conditioning expression, and Privacy Rate equation remain. The added standard MCC formula is explanatory rather than a new theoretical contribution.

C1.justification: v3's abstract attributes gains across benchmarks to tuning on only 100 examples; v2's explicit 100-example finding concerned the PRIVBENCH data-size experiment. v3 also drops the claim of introducing the first comprehensive benchmarks. The central claims about deficient privacy awareness, effective tuning, and limited general-task degradation remain.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly deems PrivAlert and Biv-Priv unsuitable as primary benchmarks and distinguishes VISPR's partial identifying attributes from its own identity-oriented categories. Appendix F newly explains why Fuyu's positive prediction bias produces high F1 but poor MCC and specificity. Most earlier mechanism explanations and limitations remain, while the expired-document qualification is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix I newly specifies five reviewers, their expertise, lack of compensation, approximate completion time, and survey instructions. Conversely, v2's explicit statement that PrivacyAlert evaluation uses its provided test set is omitted. Fine-tuning hyperparameters, hardware, training time, and restricted dataset-access arrangements remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The visual-privacy discussion adds substantive comparisons with VISPR, PicAlert, PP4AV, and ADD, sharpening the distinction between explicit identification and partial privacy attributes. MCC references are added, while CLIP and several training-data-extraction references are removed. The broader positioning around recognizing sensitive visual content remains.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion, changes the title and model terminology, and moves dataset-quality assessment into a standalone section before methodology. Appendices are reorganized into separate dataset, evaluation, and human-study sections.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a predominantly single-column layout, replaces Figure 1's radar display with benchmark bars, and splits and expands the result tables. It adds VISPR examples and human-study forms, redraws the data-size plots, and moves the Places365 ranking table into the main text. Existing appendix image galleries are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: VISPR evaluation, reporting of MCC and specificity, and fuller human-study documentation strengthen validation and reproducibility. However, v3 Table 4 introduces an unexplained pairing of MCC 0.79 and F1 0.18 for the same left-out license-plate class; v2 Table 3 reported only F1. The PDFs do not reconcile this inconsistency in the expanded generalization evidence, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
